title: AE03 - Exploring gerrymandring
text:
1. Congressional districts per state
Which state has the most congressional districts? The least? How many congressional districts are there in this state? Use functions such as table, tbl_summary or count.

gerrymander %>%
  count(state) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

# A tibble: 50 × 2
   state     n
   <chr> <int>
 1 CA       53
 2 TX       36
 3 FL       27
 4 NY       27
 5 IL       18
 6 PA       18
 7 OH       16
 8 GA       14
 9 MI       14
10 NC       13
# ℹ 40 more rows


California has the most districts at 53. Alaska, Delaware, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont, Wyoming all have 1 district.

title: AE03 - Exploring gerrymandring
text:
2. Districts at the tails
Make side-by-side box plots of percent of vote received by Trump in the 2016 Presidential Election by prevalence of gerrymandering. Identify any Congressional Districts that are potential outliers — points that fall well outside the whiskers of their box, meaning that district’s Trump vote share was unusually high or low compared to other districts with the same gerrymandering prevalence. What information can you share about them?

ggplot(gerrymander, aes(x = trump16, y = gerry)) +
  geom_boxplot() 









gerrymander %>%
  filter(gerry == "low", trump16 < 10)

# A tibble: 2 × 12
  district last_name first_name party16 clinton16 trump16 dem16 state party18
  <chr>    <chr>     <chr>      <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <chr> <chr>  
1 NY-13    Espaillat Adriano    D            92.3     5.4     1 NY    D      
2 NY-15    Serrano   Jose       D            93.8     4.9     1 NY    D      
# ℹ 3 more variables: dem18 <dbl>, flip18 <dbl>, gerry <fct>


We can see that there were two districts in NY that were outliers in the data set, both NY-13 and NY-15 which both had about 5% votes for Trump in the 2016 election.

title: AE03 - Exploring gerrymandring
text:
3. Gerrymandering and flipping
This relationship can be looked at from two directions — does gerrymandering predict a 2018 flip, and does a 2018 flip predict gerrymandering? Support both with a visualization and summary statistics. The plot answers “what does the mix look like within each group?”; the table gives the exact proportions the plot is showing. Write 1-2 bullet points about what you noticed from each plot. Use specific numbers in your answer.
Direction 1: Is a Congressional District more likely to have high prevalence of gerrymandering if a Democrat was able to flip the seat in the 2018 election? To compare the breakdown of gerrymandering prevalence within each flipped group, make sure flip18 is on the x axis and that your percents add up to 100% within each category.

ggplot(gerrymander, aes(x = factor(flip18), fill = gerry)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")







gerrymander %>%
  count(flip18, gerry)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  flip18 gerry     n
   <dbl> <fct> <int>
1     -1 low       2
2     -1 mid       3
3      0 low      52
4      0 mid     242
5      0 high     98
6      1 low       8
7      1 mid      25
8      1 high      5


Only 5 out of 38 steats were flipped that had high prevelance of gerrymandering. However nonflipped seats had a much higher rate of gerrymandering which was 98 of 392 or 25% compared to 13.2% of the flipped seats.
Direction 2: Is a Congressional District more likely to be flipped to a Democratic seat if it has high prevalence of gerrymandering, or low prevalence? Same two variables, just flipped — so now gerry is on the x-axis. Again, make sure your percents add up to 100% within each category.

ggplot(gerrymander, aes(x = gerry, fill = factor(flip18))) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")







gerrymander %>%
  count(gerry, flip18)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  gerry flip18     n
  <fct>  <dbl> <int>
1 low       -1     2
2 low        0    52
3 low        1     8
4 mid       -1     3
5 mid        0   242
6 mid        1    25
7 high       0    98
8 high       1     5


Only 4.9% of districts with high gerrymandering were flipped by Democrats in 2018 5 out of 103. However districts with low gerrymandering prevalence had 8 of 62 seats flip which is 12.9% so more than double the Democratic flip rate.

title: AE03 - Exploring gerrymandring
text:
4. Gerrymandering and presidential margin
Using mutate, create a new variable, margin16, measuring how many percentage points Clinton won or lost by in each district (clinton16 - trump16). Does gerrymandering prevalence relate to how lopsided the 2016 presidential race was in that district? Report the min, mean, and max margin by gerry level, then visualize the full distribution with a violin + boxplot combo. Describe the shape, center, and spread of each group.

gerrymander <- gerrymander %>%
  mutate(margin16 = clinton16 - trump16)

gerrymander %>%
  group_by(gerry) %>%
  summarise(min_margin = min(margin16),
            mean_margin = mean(margin16),
            max_margin = max(margin16)
            )

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  gerry min_margin mean_margin max_margin
  <fct>      <dbl>       <dbl>      <dbl>
1 low        -54.9        6.32       88.9
2 mid        -63          3.25       82.8
3 high       -63          1.34       78.2

ggplot(gerrymander, aes(x = gerry, y = margin16)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_boxplot(width = .2)

title: AE03 - Exploring gerrymandring
text:
Shape
Low: Skewed to the right the base is large with a narrow neck that stretches to high positives. Mid: Mostly symmetric, with the base being a bit larger than the neck as it extends upwards. High: Has two defined bumps the larger of the two bumps are on the negative side, overall most symmetric of all three.

title: AE03 - Exploring gerrymandring
text:
Center
Low: The center sits right at 0 which means the votes were roughly split evenly between trump and clinton Mid: The center is also sitting very close to 0 which again shows that the votes were pretty evenly distributed between the two candidates. High: The center is close to 0 however it is definitely sitting on the negative side meaning the high gerrymandered districts leaned towards trump the most.

title: AE03 - Exploring gerrymandring
text:
Spread
Low: The only spread with outliars sitting at the very top around +90 while most of the data is around -13 to +20. Mid: The spread is very uniformed, it spans from about -65 to +70 with the center falling at 0. High: Very similar spread to Mid the only thing to note is within the IQR the center is shifted below 0, meaning the votes leaned towards trump.
